subject: Biology
title: Cancer Immunotherapy
description: A quick, practical guide to Cancer Immunotherapy.

hook.text: What if your own immune system could be reprogrammed to hunt and kill cancer cells?

buildup.text: Cancer cells evade immunity by displaying 'don't eat me' signals that fool T cells.

discovery.text: Checkpoint inhibitors are drugs that unmask cancer cells, letting T cells see and attack them.

twist.text: CAR-T therapy engineers a patient's own T cells with receptors that target their specific cancer.

climax.text: Some terminal cancer patients have gone into complete remission after immunotherapy—living years longer.

punchline.text: The cure might already be inside you. It just needs a nudge.

quiz.question: What do checkpoint inhibitor drugs do?
options: Unmask cancer cells so T cells can attack them
Strengthen the skin barrier against cancer

details.summary: Cancer immunotherapy harnesses the patient's own immune system to find and destroy cancer cells. Checkpoint inhibitors release the immune system's brakes, CAR-T cell therapy engineers immune cells to target tumors, and cancer vaccines prime immunity against tumor antigens.

takeaways: Checkpoint inhibitors remove molecular brakes cancer uses to hide from immunity
CAR-T therapy engineers a patient's T cells to recognize and kill their cancer
Immunotherapy can produce durable remissions where chemotherapy could not

faq.question: How do checkpoint inhibitors work against cancer?
faq.answer: Cancers often produce proteins like PD-L1 that bind immune checkpoints on T cells, effectively telling them to stand down. Checkpoint inhibitor drugs block this interaction, removing the brakes and allowing T cells to recognize and attack the tumor.

faq.question: Why doesn't immunotherapy work for all cancers?
faq.answer: Some tumors have few mutations, making them hard for immune cells to distinguish from normal tissue. Others create immunosuppressive microenvironments or lack the inflammation needed to attract immune cells. Research aims to expand effectiveness to more cancer types.
